Wayne Swan This bill, the Treasury Legislation Amendment (Repeal Day 2015) Bill 2015, is part of a disturbing pattern that we have seen from this government not just on superannuation but, of course, in its attitude to the entitlements of people on low and middle incomes right across our country. I think it says something about this government that among its highest priorities in the super system is to make it easier for people to dodge their super guarantee obligations. This very much reflects the approach of the government to regulation, whether it is superannuation or taxation, or the intersection of the superannuation and taxation system. I think it shows a real pattern of behaviour and where the heart of this government really lies. The heart of this government really lies, I think, with an overpowered and overpaid financial and corporate elite. Basically, this government dances to their tune. The overpaid and over-empowered corporate elite are trying to, basically, pull down many of the key policy platforms that have driven growth and social mobility in our society and in our economy. Over the last 30 years, Australia has been one of the most successful developed economies when it comes to both economic growth and maintaining social mobility. The speaker opposed the Treasury Legislation Amendment (Repeal Day 2015) Bill 2015, arguing that schedule 1 would weaken penalties for employers who fail to pay superannuation on time, worsening a problem where 690,000 workers lose $2.6 billion annually due to noncompliance. They moved an amendment to reject the bill.

The speaker supported an amendment to remove schedule 1 of the Treasury Legislation Amendment (Repeal Day 2015) Bill, arguing it would reduce penalties for employers who fail to pay superannuation, affecting 690,000 Australians and costing $2.6 billion annually, and claimed the government's "simplification" rhetoric masks cuts to worker protections.

The speaker argued that the government's regulatory reform agenda has been a success, exceeding its red tape reduction target by finding $4.5 billion over two years. They announced support for the Treasury Legislation Amendment (Repeal Day 2015) Bill, highlighted a $263.5 million boost for on-farm irrigation in southern New South Wales, and criticised Labor’s handling of foreign investment, particularly the Archer Daniels Midland bid for GrainCorp and the S. Kidman & Co. sale.

The speaker argued for the Treasury Legislation Amendment (Repeal Day 2015) Bill 2015 as a measure to reduce red tape and remove unnecessary legislation, criticising the previous Labor government for passing 975 acts and 39,000 pages of legislation. Specific positions included supporting free trade agreements with Japan, South Korea, China, and the Trans-Pacific Partnership, privatising Medibank Private, and reforming superannuation guarantee charges and unclaimed superannuation for terminally ill patients.

The speaker supported the Treasury Legislation Amendment (Repeal Day 2015) Bill, announcing $2.45 billion in red‑tape savings, and argued that compulsory superannuation harms small‑business startups and young people’s ability to enter the housing market.

The speaker argued the Treasury Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 reflects a government pattern of prioritising tax avoidance for wealthy elites over fairness for low- and middle-income Australians. Concrete claims include that over one-third of corporate entities paid no tax, lost corporate tax revenue totals at least $26 billion over four years, and the effective corporate tax rate is 24 cents per dollar, not the nominal 30 percent.

The speaker moved amendments to block the repeal of superannuation guarantee charge provisions, arguing the bill would weaken penalties for employers and harm 690,000 workers who miss out on $2.6 billion in superannuation each year.
